newsitem.title: India: OPINION - THE POLITICAL DRAMA - James Capel B&K.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - THE POLITICAL DRAMA - James Capel B&K.

text.p: THE POLITICAL DRAMA: DOES POLITICS MATTER? - James
Capel B&K, Sanjeev Mohta.
THE POLITICAL DRAMA:
DOES POLITICS MATTER?

The current political impasse will have a short-term impact on the economy. There will be postponement of some key economic decisions such as measures on infrastructure as also consumption and investment decisions. However, if the budget goes through in its entirety, despite the collapse of the government, India will have reached a stage where the economy will be relatively less affected by the turbulent state of political affairs, and by which political party is at the helm. Market reaction in the past few days vindicates this thesis. While the depoliticisation of the Indian economy itself calls for a rerating of the Indian market, the current uncertainty offers a good opportunity for long-term investors.
WHAT IS THE ECONOMIC IMPACT OF THE CURRENT POLITICAL CRISIS?
Depending on how long the current impasse will continue, the economy will be affected in the short term. The key decisions which will not be taken as long as the uncertainty continues are:
* The oil price hike
* Disinvestment
* Measures on infrastructure

Also, there may be a lack of consumer and business confidence, which will result in decisions being postponed. This would make the current slowdown last longer than what we had envisaged. However, we continue to be bullish in the medium/long term if the budget is passed.

While we had believed that the market would not react negatively to the announcement of worse-than-expected results, this may not be the case, as the good news may be postponed. Thus, we believe that till there is a clearer signal, the (Bombay Stock Exchange) market will remain in a trading range of 3400-3800 in the short term. The uncertainty, however, should be capitalised on by long-term investors, as we are bullish in the medium/long term.
The silver lining to these dark political clouds is the fact that the Indian economy is going through a slow but steady depoliticisation.
DEPOLITICISATION OF THE INDIAN ECONOMY: THE MARKET SAYS IT ALL:
DURING THE DECEMBER'94 CRISIS, THE MARKET WAS JITTERY...

In December'94, there was a political crisis of sorts when the Congress party lost the elections in a big way, in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. The market reacted very negatively amidst concerns that if the Congress fell, the reforms may not continue.
....IN THE CURRENT POLITICAL CRISIS, WHICH IS MUCH WORSE, THE MARKET IS FAR LESS CONCERNED:

Market movement in the past few days confirms our theory of depoliticisation of the economy. We do not ever remember the market bouncing back so strongly in the midst of a political crisis. The only reason for this, we feel, is that the market was hopeful, whatever be the outcome of the crisis, the budget will go through (which seems to be coming true).
The depoliticisation of the Indian economy started in a major way only in 1991 under the Congress regime, with the announcement of reforms.
GREATER CONSENSUS ON THE ECONOMIC FRONT:

Over the past five years, all political parties unanimously seem to have embraced the reforms process with equal zest. This is clearly evident at the state level. Despite being ruled by a wide variety of political parties, most states have been actively pursuing the liberalisation process, and vigorously courting foreign investment. Thus, any change at the centre no longer results in any dramatic change in the economic policy.

At the centre, the party which was considered the 'worst case' from the economic point of view has almost become the 'best case' today. Economic reforms have continued in the past few months, the high point of which was the superb Budget. Even after the Congress withdrew support, we have seen the announcement of a liberal EXIM Policy.
CHANGES IN ATTITUDES:

The structural changes in reforms, initiated in 1991, have started having an impact on the attitudes of decision makers - the bureaucracy, and the people. While the impact has taken its time, and is still not omnipresent, the direction is clear. And this is what makes us bullish on the future. Some of the issues which clearly indicate depoliticisation are:
* Delicensing of most of the sectors in the new economic policy.
* Dilution of Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices and Foreign Exchange Regulation Act.
* Increasing importance of committees (the Chelliah Committee for instance).
* Increasing strength of the Judiciary (number of politicians being indicted by the courts has increased).
* Bodies such as Central Bureau of investigation and Securities and Exchange Board of India ar increasingly gaining teeth.
* Banks and financial institutions becoming more 'independent' in sanctioning of loans.
* RBI getting more autonomous (for example scrapping of adhoc T-bills).
* Public sector units (PSUs) are becoming more independent/efficient.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
